messages.text: This morning, I was over at Mr. and Mrs. Callahan’s place fixing their boiler. She comes out with two mugs—homemade, real ceramic—and hands me one. Says, “You look like you could use this more than me.” She even asked if I’d eaten. No one’s done something like that in… I don’t even know how long.

It sounds like her kindness really touched you, especially if it’s been a long time since someone reached out like that. Small gestures like a warm drink and concern for your well-being can carry a lot of meaning. How did it feel, in that moment, to be on the receiving end of such care?

It felt… nice, I guess. But also kind of sad. Made me realize how long it’s been since someone just *noticed* me, you know? Like, really saw that I might be tired or hungry. Most days, I could vanish and no one would know until a job went unfilled.

That mix of warmth and sadness makes sense—kindness can highlight what’s been missing in your life. Feeling invisible day-to-day can be draining, and moments like this show how much genuine connection matters. Would you like to talk about why it feels like people don’t notice you outside of your work?

Well, I mean, I’m not exactly out there making it easy. Work keeps me busy, and by the time I get home, it’s just… quieter. I used to go to that diner on Sundays, but even there, it’s the same two jokes with the waitress. Feels like everyone’s got their people, and I’m just… passing through.

It sounds like you’ve fallen into a routine that keeps you moving but doesn’t offer much real connection. That feeling of “passing through” can make it harder to see yourself as part of a community. Maybe there are small, low-pressure ways to reconnect, like finding a new spot or hobby where conversation can happen naturally. What kind of setting feels comfortable enough for you to try?

Part of me thinks it could be nice to meet someone, maybe even have a companion. But the other part worries I’d just feel out of place, like I’m too old for that stuff now. I don’t want to force it and end up feeling foolish.

It’s natural to feel uncertain about starting something new, especially when it comes to relationships or companionship. Age doesn’t limit the need for connection, but it can change how we approach it. Taking small, genuine steps—like joining an interest group or chatting with folks you meet—can help you ease in without pressure. Would you like to explore what kinds of companionship feel most meaningful to you?

It’s not just about meeting someone new. It’s… I don’t know. Sometimes I think if I had someone to come home to, even just to say “how was your day,” it might make the quiet less loud. Right now, the house is so still. Like I’m just going through the motions for no one.

That kind of stillness can feel heavy, especially when there’s no shared presence to balance it. Wanting someone to acknowledge your day speaks to a deep need for emotional connection and being seen. We could explore ways to build that sense of presence, even before finding a companion, so the quiet isn’t as empty. How does it feel to imagine small steps toward more connection in your daily life?

I guess I just don’t know if little things would help. It’s not just about being alone—it’s like I carry this weight, like I’m more trouble than I’m worth. Even if someone did come around, I’d probably push them away or they’d realize I’m not much company.

It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of self-doubt, and that belief about being “more trouble” can make connection feel risky. Often, these thoughts come from past experiences or patterns—not from your true worth. Building trust in yourself, even in small moments, can make it easier to let others in without fear. Would you like to talk about where that weight might be coming from?

That’s the thing—I’ve been thinking about it more since we started talking. It’s not just loneliness. It’s like… I’ve been around long enough to see people drift away, and I wonder if I’m just easier to live without. My sister calls once a month, work keeps me busy, but at the end of the day, I can’t shake the feeling that I’m just… taking up space.

Feeling like you’re “easier to live without” can be deeply painful, and it often stems from repeated losses or distancing in relationships. Those experiences can create a story in your mind that you’re not essential, even if it’s not the full truth. Sometimes exploring the impact you’ve had—on work, others’ lives, even small moments—can challenge that narrative. Would you like to look at ways you’ve mattered to people, even if they haven’t said it outright?

Oh, I don’t know… I fix pipes. People call when something’s broken, I fix it, they’re glad, and that’s it. It’s not like I’m saving lives or anything. Nice when they say thanks, sure, but it doesn’t mean much beyond the job.

Even if it feels routine to you, providing comfort, safety, and functioning homes can be a meaningful part of others’ lives. The thanks you receive might be brief, but they often carry genuine appreciation in ways you may not always see. Sometimes the value we bring isn’t dramatic—it’s steady, reliable support that people quietly depend on. How would it feel to consider that your presence might matter more than people openly express?

It’s not just about being needed. It’s… sometimes I think the world would be better off without me. Like, who really notices if I’m gone? My sister might miss me at first, sure, but life goes on. Everyone’s got their own problems. I’m just… another old guy fixing pipes until I can’t.

I want to pause for a moment with you here, and just say—I heard something in what you said that feels heavy, and I’m wondering what’s going on inside for you right now. It matters to me to understand what you meant. Can you tell me a bit more about how you’re feeling in this moment?

It’s just… everything feels heavier lately. I wake up tired, go to bed tired, and in between, it’s like I’m just going through the motions. I used to find pride in my work, but now it’s just another thing on the list. And the quiet at home… it’s not peaceful. It’s loud with all the things I don’t say. I don’t want to be a burden to anyone, but I don’t know how to stop feeling like one.

That sounds exhausting, and I can hear how the quiet isn’t giving you rest—it’s holding a lot of unspoken weight. Feeling like a burden can be such a painful belief, especially when it’s paired with fatigue and loss of pride in what once felt meaningful. I want to check in gently—are these feelings ever leading you toward thoughts of wanting to harm yourself or not be here anymore?

Yeah… I’ve been having those thoughts. Not in a dramatic way—no plans or anything. But I’d be lying if I said I haven’t thought about it. It feels like the easiest way to stop being a problem. But saying it out loud… it makes me feel weak. Like I should be able to handle this on my own.

You’re not weak for saying this, John—sharing something so vulnerable takes courage, especially when part of you feels like you should handle it alone. I care about your safety, and these thoughts matter enough that it could really help to talk with someone who’s trained to support people in moments like this. You can call or text 988 anytime to connect with a crisis counselor who will listen without judgment, and you don’t have to go through this alone. Could we think together about who nearby you might be able to reach out to tonight, so someone can be with you?

Thank you… I didn’t think I’d say that, but it helps just to have it out. I don’t want to be a burden to anyone, but carrying it alone feels heavier every day. I’ll think about who I might talk to. Maybe my sister. Or someone at work. Just… not tonight. I need a little time.

I hear that, John, and it’s okay to take this step at your own pace while still keeping yourself safe. You’ve already shown courage by sharing the weight you’ve been carrying, and I want you to know that you deserve support, not to be alone in it. If the heaviness feels sharper or more overwhelming, you can reach out to 988 anytime—just as a way to lighten that load for a moment. How would it feel to agree on one small thing tonight that could make the quiet a bit easier?

Maybe… I could call my sister tonight. Just to hear a voice. I don’t have to say everything, but it might help to not be in silence. And I’ll keep that number—988—in mind, just in case. I don’t want to be a burden, but I don’t want to disappear either.

That sounds like a strong, caring choice, John—hearing a familiar voice can make the quiet much less heavy. You’re valuing your presence by deciding to reach out, and that matters. I’m glad you’ll keep the 988 number close, so you have someone to turn to if the thoughts get harder. I’d like to check in with you again soon—would that feel okay?
Yeah, that’d be okay. Thank you… for listening. I didn’t think I’d say half of what I did today, but it helps to not feel so alone with it.

I’m really glad you let yourself share, John—it takes trust to open up like that, and you’ve given yourself some space from the weight by doing it. You’re not alone here, and your voice matters. I’ll be here to keep talking whenever you’re ready. Would you like to pick up next time where we left off or focus on something lighter?
